nodes.label: Simple Harmonic Motion
nodes.note: SHM is motion under a restoring acceleration proportional to displacement: $$a = -\omega^2 x$$. Its energy oscillates between kinetic and potential forms.

nodes.label: SHM Fundamentals
nodes.note: The defining condition is linear restoring force: $$F = -kx \Rightarrow a = -\frac{k}{m}x$$.

nodes.label: Defining Condition
nodes.note: Acceleration is always directed toward the mean position and proportional to displacement: $$a = -\omega^2 x$$. Any system satisfying this oscillates in SHM.

nodes.label: Differential Equation of SHM
nodes.note: $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \omega^2 x = 0$$ with solution $$x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$. The angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$.

nodes.label: Displacement, Velocity, Acceleration
nodes.note: $$v = A\omega\cos(\omega t + \phi), \ a = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$. Maximum speed at mean position: $$v_{max} = A\omega$$; maximum acceleration at extremes: $$a_{max} = A\omega^2$$.

nodes.label: Kinematics Example
nodes.note: For $x = 2\sin(3t)$ cm: $A = 2\ \text{cm}$, $\omega = 3\ \text{rad/s}$, so $$v_{max} = A\omega = 6\ \text{cm/s}, \ a_{max} = A\omega^2 = 18\ \text{cm/s}^2$$.

nodes.label: Phase and Reference Circle
nodes.note: $$x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$ maps to projection of uniform circular motion of radius $A$ and angular speed $\omega$. Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$.

nodes.label: Time Period and Frequency
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \ f = \frac{1}{T}, \ \omega = 2\pi f$$. Period is independent of amplitude for ideal SHM.

nodes.label: Period Example
nodes.note: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ mass on a $200\ \text{N/m}$ spring: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.5/200} \approx 0.31\ \text{s}$$.

nodes.label: Energy in SHM
nodes.note: Total mechanical energy is conserved and fixed by amplitude: $$E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$$.

nodes.label: Kinetic Energy
nodes.note: $$K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$$. It is maximum at the mean position and zero at extremes.

nodes.label: KE at Half Amplitude
nodes.note: At $x = A/2$: $$K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2\left(A^2 - \frac{A^2}{4}\right) = \frac{3}{4}E$$. Three-quarters of the energy is kinetic there.

nodes.label: Potential Energy
nodes.note: $$U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2$$. Stored energy grows quadratically with displacement from equilibrium.

nodes.label: Point Where K Equals U
nodes.note: Setting $K = U$ gives $$x = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$$. At this point half the energy is kinetic and half potential.

nodes.label: Double-Frequency Energy Oscillation
nodes.note: Both $K$ and $U$ vary as $\sin^2$ or $\cos^2$, so each pulsates at twice the SHM frequency: $$f_{energy} = 2f_{SHM}$$.

nodes.label: Time-Average vs Position-Average Energy
nodes.note: Time-averaged over a cycle, $$\langle K \rangle = \langle U \rangle = \frac{E}{2}$$. Position-averaged over the path from $-A$ to $A$ gives a different split, a classic trap.

nodes.label: Spring-Mass Systems
nodes.note: Spring networks reduce to one equivalent constant. For springs, $$k = \frac{F}{x}$$ and $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_{eq}}}$$.

nodes.label: Springs in Series
nodes.note: $$\frac{1}{k_{eq}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$$. Equivalent constant is smaller, so the period increases.

nodes.label: Series Example
nodes.note: Two $100\ \text{N/m}$ springs in series give $k_{eq} = 50\ \text{N/m}$. A $2\ \text{kg}$ mass then oscillates with $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{2/50} \approx 1.26\ \text{s}$$.

nodes.label: Springs in Parallel
nodes.note: $$k_{eq} = k_1 + k_2$$. Stiffness adds, shortening the period.

nodes.label: Spring Cutting Rule
nodes.note: Cutting a spring into $n$ equal parts makes each part $n$ times stiffer: $$k' = nk$$. Shorter springs stretch less for the same force.

nodes.label: Two-Body Oscillator and Reduced Mass
nodes.note: Two masses on a spring oscillate with $$\mu = \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{k}}$$. This collapses the two-body problem to one effective body.

nodes.label: Vertical Spring-Mass SHM
nodes.note: Gravity only shifts the equilibrium by $$x_0 = \frac{mg}{k}$$. Oscillation about the new equilibrium obeys $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$$, unchanged.

nodes.label: Pendulum Dynamics
nodes.note: A pendulum is SHM for small angles. The simple pendulum period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$.

nodes.label: Simple Pendulum
nodes.note: For small angular displacement, restoring torque gives $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$. Period grows with length and shrinks with gravity.

nodes.label: Seconds Pendulum
nodes.note: A pendulum with $T = 2\ \text{s}$ needs $$L = \frac{gT^2}{4\pi^2} \approx 0.994\ \text{m}$$. It is the classic seconds pendulum.

nodes.label: Pendulum in Accelerating Frames
nodes.note: In a lift accelerating at $a$, use $g_{eff} = g \pm a$: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{eff}}}$$. Free fall ($a = g$) gives infinite period.

nodes.label: Physical (Compound) Pendulum
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}$$, where $I$ is moment of inertia about the pivot and $d$ is pivot-to-COM distance. It generalizes the simple pendulum.

nodes.label: Torsional Pendulum
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{\kappa}}$$, with $\kappa$ the torsional constant of the wire. Used to measure moments of inertia.

nodes.label: Large-Angle Correction
nodes.note: For amplitude $\theta_0$, the period lengthens: $$T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\left(1 + \frac{\theta_0^2}{16}\right)$$. Small-angle formula underestimates $T$.

nodes.label: Pendulum in a Lift
nodes.note: Downward acceleration $a$ reduces effective gravity: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g - a}}$$. Upward acceleration increases it; $a = g$ downward freezes the pendulum.

nodes.label: Superposition, Damping, Resonance
nodes.note: SHMs combine by superposition; real oscillators lose energy and respond to driving. Resonance occurs when $$\omega_{drive} = \omega_0$$.

nodes.label: Superposition of Collinear SHMs
nodes.note: Two same-frequency SHMs give a single SHM: $$A' = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\phi}$$. Phase difference $\phi$ decides constructive or destructive addition.

nodes.label: Superposition Example
nodes.note: Two equal SHMs $x_1 = A\sin\omega t$, $x_2 = A\sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$ add to $$A' = \sqrt{A^2 + A^2} = A\sqrt{2}$$ with phase lead $\pi/4$.

nodes.label: Lissajous Figures
nodes.note: Perpendicular SHMs trace Lissajous patterns whose shape depends on the frequency ratio and phase. Equal frequencies with $\pi/2$ phase give a circle or ellipse: $$\frac{x^2}{A^2} + \frac{y^2}{B^2} = 1$$.

nodes.label: Damped Harmonic Motion
nodes.note: $$x = A_0 e^{-bt/2m}\cos(\omega' t + \phi), \ \omega' = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \frac{b^2}{4m^2}}$$. Amplitude decays exponentially while frequency drops slightly.

nodes.label: Damping Time Constant
nodes.note: Amplitude halves when $e^{-bt/2m} = 1/2$, i.e. $$t_{1/2} = \frac{2m\ln 2}{b}$$. Energy falls four times faster.

nodes.label: Forced Oscillations and Resonance
nodes.note: A driven oscillator peaks in amplitude when driving frequency matches natural frequency: $$A_{max} \text{ at } \omega = \omega_0$$. Light damping gives a sharp, tall resonance peak.

nodes.label: Resonance Condition
nodes.note: A swing pushed at its natural frequency $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g/L}$ grows in amplitude even with small pushes. Pushing off-frequency yields small response.

nodes.label: Quality Factor
nodes.note: $$Q = \frac{\omega_0 m}{b}$$ measures sharpness of resonance and energy stored per cycle lost. High $Q$ means light damping and a narrow bandwidth.
